purpose: Molindone is used to treat schizophrenia, a mental health condition that can cause hallucinations, delusions, and confused thinking. It helps reduce these symptoms so you can think more clearly and feel more like yourself. It may also help with agitation and disorganized behavior.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a chemical messenger called dopamine to send signals between nerve cells. In schizophrenia, dopamine activity can become overactive in certain areas of the brain. Molindone works by blocking dopamine receptors, which helps calm down that overactivity and reduces symptoms like hearing voices or having unusual beliefs.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling sleepy, dizziness when standing up too quickly, dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and restlessness or difficulty sitting still. Some people may notice stiffness or muscle tremors similar to Parkinson's disease symptoms. Unlike many other antipsychotics, molindone is less likely to cause weight gain.
warnings: Important: This medication can cause a serious movement disorder called tardive dyskinesia — uncontrollable movements of the face, tongue, or body — especially with long-term use. Tell your doctor right away if you notice unusual movements. It can also cause a rare but dangerous condition called Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS), with symptoms like high fever, muscle stiffness, and confusion — seek emergency care immediately if this happens. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication. Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis should not use this drug due to increased risk of death. Tell your doctor about all your medications, as many drugs can interact with molindone.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose for adults is around 50 to 75 mg per day, taken in divided doses throughout the day. Your doctor may adjust your dose depending on how you respond, typically ranging from 15 mg up to 225 mg per day for more severe symptoms. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes and do not stop suddenly without talking to your doctor first.
